_provenance.primary_source: International Pacific Halibut Commission (IPHC) — Annual Data Reports & Technical Reports
secondary_sources: Clark, W.G. & Hare, S.R. (2002). Effects of size-at-age changes on halibut stock assessment and yield predictions. IPHC Scientific Report No. 82.
Stewart, I.J. & Hicks, A.C. (2018). Spatial survey and assessment models for Pacific halibut.
_provenance.notes: One of the most remarkable biological phenomena in North Pacific fisheries is the ~50% drop in Pacific halibut weight-at-age between 1980 and 2012. A 12-year-old female halibut weighed approximately 45 lbs in 1988, but only 18 lbs in 2012. IPHC research attributes this decline to a combination of intra- and inter-specific competition (high total flatfish biomass), ocean climate shifts (PDO positive phases), and selective fishing pressure. Size-at-age has stabilized and shown mild increases since 2015.

hypothesized_mechanisms.evidence: High total biomass of Arrowtooth flounder and flatfish in the Bering Sea / GOA competing for benthic prey (polychaetes, crabs, small fish).
Positive PDO phases alter zooplankton and forage fish composition, reducing high-fat prey availability during critical juvenile growth years.
Decades of minimum size limits (32 inches) selectively removing the fastest-growing individuals before they reproduce.
